extracted.intended_audience: general readers and scholars interested in media criticism, media literacy, and contemporary journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Daniel Boorstin’s criteria to recognize and evaluate 'pseudo-events' and related phenomena in modern digital media and news — distinguishing manufactured happenings, propaganda, and manufactured celebrity from genuine news and achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not spontaneous — planned, planted, or incited
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudo-event 'is not spontaneous, but comes about because someone has planned, planted, or incited it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: film and music awards shows are constructed events created to be reported on; the nominated products already exist and are now given marketing campaigns to generate news coverage. Anti-pattern: treating staged publicity stunts as naturally occurring news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planted primarily to be reported or reproduced
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudo-event is 'planted primarily (not always exclusively) for the immediate purpose of being reported or reproduced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: university campaigns, slogans, and public events that puff prestige more than demonstrate real accomplishment (linked to college admissions scandals). Scoring note: if the primary aim of an event is publicity rather than substantive action, it qualifies as a pseudo-event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to underlying reality is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudo-event’s 'relation to the underlying reality of the situation is ambiguous' — the purpose of the event is either unclear or deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to test whether an event accurately reflects or meaningfully connects to real conditions. Anti-pattern: reporting on events whose connection to factual circumstances cannot be verified or is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended to be a self‑fulfilling prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudo-event is usually 'intended to be a self-fulfilling prophecy' where those who create the event are the primary beneficiaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: labeling a book a 'best seller' to generate sales regardless of transparent sales data. Scoring note: assess who benefits and whether the event's reported importance is created rather than earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate pseudo-events from propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Boorstin differentiates: '[w]hile a pseudo-event is an ambiguous truth, propaganda is an appealing falsehood. […] Propaganda oversimplifies experience, pseudo-events overcomplicate it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: a televised presidential debate (pseudo-event feeding the duty to be educated) versus a political speech (which may be propagandistic and inflame). Use this distinction when evaluating intent and truthfulness of messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of manufactured celebrity and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that celebrity/influence is manufactured include purchasing followers, meticulously manufacturing glitz and glamour, and creating content solely to attract attention (e.g., unboxing videos, influencer shilling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: HBO's Fake Famous shows how followers and profiles can be fabricated. Use these signs to judge whether 'influence' reflects meaningful insight or merely traffic-generation; note Twitter's verification threshold as an example of a metric divorced from substantive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness should not be determined by filling news-cycle gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary when the supply-and-demand pressures of the news cycle lead to filling gaps with constructed happenings rather than essential stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: evaluate whether coverage exists because a story is genuinely important or because producers need something 'groundbreaking' to report daily. Anti-pattern: prioritizing eye-catching 'content' that serves attention metrics over informational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic curation and user‑curated reality as a reason for skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'the more we click on certain types of information, the more of it we see,' algorithmic and user-curated feeds narrow experience and create information bubbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation step: check whether content prominence is driven by algorithmic amplification or by organic significance; seek diverse sources to counteract echo chambers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on work/achievement rather than personality or well‑knownness
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It focuses on the personality rather than on the work. It puts a premium on well-knownness for its own sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge cultural coverage and celebrity: prioritize substantive accomplishment over fame-for-fame's-sake. Anti-pattern: treating notoriety or name recognition as equivalent to merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media‑literacy remedies — awareness and reinvigoration of honest conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial criterion: counter pseudo-events and propaganda by cultivating media literacy, being aware of 'shadow casters,' and reinvigorating honest conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: educate audiences to recognize manufactured events, encourage critical discussion over quick outrage, and value sources that reveal underlying facts rather than amplifying spectacle.
